doc.title: Hal Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Defining swing and playing with the beat
summary: Swing as lightness and elasticity; adjusting to each rhythm section, such as Dave McKenna.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: If you had to — tough question number one, okay — if you had a young drummer, defining swing, can you do it in words?

It’s a feeling of lightness and elasticity and working with the other members of the rhythm section, where it’s a joint effort to move forward, but it’s not tense. It doesn’t fall back on the beat. It can get in the groove, but it doesn’t just sit there, it keeps moving. But not too far ahead and not too far behind. That’s the ideal I think.
Playing ahead of the beat, and playing behind the beat — is this something that exists for you?

Depending on the band. I try to scope out a rhythm section right away. And if I can hear one guy, if the bass is turned way up, and he’s going to have it his way or no way, I’m not going to fight him. Because then we’re going to drown out everybody on the horns, and they’re going to be mad at both of us. So I’ll try and work with him. If he’s going to work with me, or if there’s no amp, or if everybody’s trying to make a group effort out of © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

it, then sometimes I’ll lead the way. I have to know who I’m working with. If it’s people I don’t work with all the time, like Dave McKenna this weekend, I haven’t worked with him for a long time. I listen to him. I didn’t want to put my foot on his chest and say okay, here’s where it is. I want him to be comfortable. If it’s someone I work with all the time, they know what I do anyway, and they’re probably going to wait for me to lay it down.
